articles.title: Last known North East sword maker hopes to pass on craft
articles.summary: Frank Lee believes he is the only person making the swords so integral to the North East.
articles.body:
The tradition of rapper sword dancing developed on the coalfields of north-east England as early as the 18th Century. While dance troops continue to entertain audiences across the world, it is believed 81-year-old Frank Lee, from Cumbria, is now the last maker of the swords so integral to the dance.

Retired professor of cultural studies Trish Winter says rapper sword dancing, using two-handled bending swords, was a "North East story".

Developed in the mining communities of Northumberland and County Durham, Winter says it evolved due to lay offs in the mines over winter when miners were forced to find other ways to make money.

"There were traditions of sword dancing around Europe from the Middle Ages," she said.

"But rapper develops on the coalfields, presumably, from existing practices of sword dancing, to something very unique and very particular to the coalfields."

The dance troops are made up of at least five men, each connected by flexible rapper swords. The dance is fast and the men weave in and out of each other and moving around the swords.

While the dance is traditionally performed by men, there are modern examples of female troops.

"Most people are familiar with colliery banners and brass bands as part of the North East industrial heritage," Winter says.

"And rapper dancing is just as much a part of that heritage, but I think it's less well known.

"I think it's actually a really good example of how industrial heritage isn't just about buildings and machinery."

Lee started making swords in 1977, albeit sporadically.

A former dancer himself, he first came across the tradition when he was 12 years old.

"I was just totally wrapped up in it," says Lee.

"It's fascinating to watch, it's got an element of conjuring in it, it's got fast movement, it's complex, it's got music involved in it, and it's got comedy involved in it."

The former craft, design and technology teacher started making the swords more regularly years later out of "necessity".

"At the time they were quite difficult to get and I have the wherewithal to make them," Lee says.

And he believes the popularity is growing.

"I'm quite surprised it isn't much better known than it is, but it's been getting better now over the last few decades," Lee says.

"I think when I started in 1977 there might have been about 20 teams in the whole country.

"And I'm just about to make my 500th set of rappers."

So while the form of dancing is far from a dying art, the same cannot be said for the art of rapper sword making.

This is the motivation behind Amble-based Dry Water Arts' latest project to try and preserve Lee's knowledge.

The project, which is fronted by Winter, has received a grant from The National Lottery Heritage Fund to preserve the craft for future generations.

"The first thing we want to do is to safeguard the craft," Winter said.

"Because Frank Lee is the last known maker of rapper swords.

"We realised there was a danger that that knowledge would disappear before it had been passed on."

Part of the project involves a film documenting how Lee makes swords.

"I suppose the concern at the moment is that there isn't anybody on the horizon that looks like they might want to take over, and there's not enough worldwide demands to justify a commercial set up," Lee says.

"Everybody who's ever made them has always been the last of the rapper-makers and I'm just the current last of the rapper-makers.

"But I am 81 now and at some point my body's going to say enough."

Winter says: "We want to document his knowledge for the future in the hope there will be future makers of rapper swords.

"The big sort of paradox is that the rapper sword dance is very much alive all over the world and it's a vibrant lively dance tradition.

"But the craft that it relies on is held in the knowledge of one person, so there's a point of vulnerability there."

The project officially launches on the 15 November at Dry Waters Art Centre with an exhibition.

It then runs until September 2027 and includes talks and demonstrations from Lee, workshops and performances.

"The project isn't going to completely solve the problem," Winter says.

"But what it will do is document Frank's knowledge so it is saved."

articles.title: Birmingham student's dresses worn by the stars at national awards
articles.summary: Strictly dancer Lauren Oakley and singer Elle Exxe wore the designs at the Pride of Britain Awards.
articles.body:
From the university classroom to the red carpet - a Birmingham fashion student's designs have been donned by the stars at a national awards event.

Final year student Rohan Scott said "words can't describe the excitement" after his dresses were worn by Strictly Come Dancing professional Lauren Oakley and singer-songwriter Elle Exxe at the Pride of Britain Awards.

The 22-year-old student from Birmingham City University (BCU) created the eye-catching outfits as part of a collection during his second year of study.

He described working with the pair as a "wholesome experience", adding that they were both "warm, welcoming and down to earth".

Rohan said: "I feel an immense feeling of gratitude that I've been considered in this way by someone outside of the classroom.

"Having this large exposure is exciting and terrifying at the same time, and it's an experience that I'll be eternally grateful for."

The red-carpet moment came at the awards ceremony on Monday after both women were impressed by the university's emerging designers at previous fashion events.

Professional dancer Oakley, who grew up in Birmingham, hosted BCU's annual graduate fashion show, 1000 Threads, earlier this year. She said she wanted to use her platform on Strictly Come Dancing to showcase local talent on a national stage.

"Growing up in Birmingham myself, you're quite aware that creatively a lot of things happen in London, so taking the opportunity to use my platform to help someone local in the creative industry was really important to me," she said.

Oakley added that all four dresses Scott brought for her to try on were "stunning".

Meanwhile, Elle Exxe discovered the university's designers at BCU's 2026 London Fashion Week showcase at Somerset House.

She praised Scott for making her feel calm and confident during a fitting and said his warmth and talent were a rare combination.

"Judging by the reaction I got from the attendees last night, Rohan's going to have superstars falling over themselves to wear his designs on the red carpet," she added.

The success was welcomed by BCU's fashion department. Course leader and senior lecturer Dean Fallon said the opportunity was testament to Scott's skill and drive.

His work, Fallon added, already showed "a strong sense of identity and positioning".

For Scott, two red-carpet appearances at one of Britain's best-known awards ceremonies offered a glimpse of what could lie ahead and a rather glamorous addition to his student portfolio.

articles.title: Manx designer inspired by island's folklore and history
articles.summary: Bethany Williams's latest fashion collection is inspired by Manx folklore and history.
articles.body:
An artist and designer from the Isle of Man has used the island's history, folklore and heritage as inspiration for a new collection featured in British Vogue.

Bethany Williams, from Douglas, built her career in sustainable fashion in London before returning to the island to recover from a chronic illness.

Since moving back, she has reconnected with her roots, drawing on Manx culture and traditions in her latest designs.

She said: "I kind of had two separate worlds. It's been really nice with this project to bring them both together."

The 16-piece collection transforms discarded clothing into wearable artworks, combining Williams's own paintings with crochet, patchwork and traditional Manx craft techniques.

Called The Light We Carry, Williams said the collection explores how light changes through the seasons, as well as the light people carry within themselves.

"Light exists within all of us, even if sometimes it feels distant or dimmed. It can be something that we can be guided back to," she said.

In 2013, Williams was diagnosed with new daily persistent headache (NDPH), a condition that causes severe facial and head pain. After a period of remission, it returned in 2022 with more severe symptoms, leaving her bedbound.

During her recovery on the Isle of Man, Williams was drawn back to painting the Manx landscape, something she had not done since studying for a foundation degree at University College Isle of Man.

The 36-year-old said: "I felt like the landscape of the Isle of Man really brought me back to myself."

"I felt like that has been a really integral part for me, being in nature."

Williams also drew on her family history when developing the collection, using the shapes and silhouettes of clothes passed down from her great-great-grandparents, including a dress dating from the 1920s.

"I was looking at how love never leaves, it just changes form," she said.

Featured in British Vogue, the collection marks a return to fashion for Williams, whose experience of chronic illness has changed both her outlook on life and her approach to making art.

Reflecting on her illness and reconnection with the Isle of Man, she said she was now "making work that's maybe more personal to me... about the human experience".

articles.title: The West Country's 'most haunted' pubs and hotels where guests cannot explain encounters
articles.summary: Ahead of Halloween, we have compiled some of the most popular haunted stories in pubs and hotels.
articles.body:
Several pubs and hotels across the West Country have been rumoured to be haunted by ghosts for centuries.

Guests staying in the historic venues claim to experience strange noises and sounds, with one encounter even convincing a TV presenter that there is "definitely life after death".

Ahead of Halloween, we have compiled some of the most popular haunted stories from across the region.

The Llandoger Trow on King Street in Bristol dates back to the 17th Century and there have been multiple reports of it being haunted by 15 ghosts.

The pub is also rumoured to have been visited by Blackbeard, a pirate who was rumoured to set fire to his own beard in battle in order to appear even more ferocious.

Staff and visitors have reported hearing unexpected footsteps and eerie noises.

Some of the reported ghosts at the pub have been given names, including Pierre, who allegedly walks with a pained limp and a caliper on one leg.

He is often seen staring mournfully from the upstairs windows at the living patrons in the street below, according to Visit Bristol.

The Shoemakers Museum in Street, Somerset, is housed in a 16th Century manor called the Grange.

According to Sam Cullen, manager at the museum, the site is "super-duper haunted".

She said the memoir Tales of the Polden Hills, by Frances Wood, written in 1922, describes supernatural occurrences.

"This was during a time when people loved a ghost story, when the unknown and creepy was exciting for folk," Cullen said.

She said one of the stories tells of two brothers who lived in the manor, one of whom reported seeing a white dog in the kitchen.

"A few moments later the other brother came running in and told the exact same tale," Cullen said.

"The only difference was that in this retelling the dog got up and left the room via the door. And the boy was like, 'how did the dog leave, the door was locked?'

"Within three weeks their father died in his study."

Cullen said when she started working at the museum, she did not know about the history.

"I thought it was just an abandoned old building," she said.

"All of the sudden, this disinfectant hospital smell came out of nowhere," she added.

"I asked, 'why does it smells like hospitals in the barn?'

"It turns out it used to be used as a quarantine hospital during the Spanish flu," she added.

Yvette Fielding, who presents the TV programme Most Haunted, said the Ancient Ram Inn in Wotton-under-Edge in Gloucestershire "sticks in her mind" as one of the most haunted places she visited while filming the show.

She added: "When I first started, I wasn't sure what to believe and now I know there's life after death and I'm not scared of death at all.

"Stuart [Fielding's colleague] decided he wasn't going to be respectful and he was swearing and saying, 'do your worst'.

"Later on in the early hours of the morning, Stuart said he felt fists like he was being beaten. The next day he had bruises around his body and he lost his hair - alopecia - through the stress of it all."

The Ancient Ram Inn has been hosting paranormal investigations throughout October.

On Halloween night, the pub will host an overnight ghost hunt, where people can come in fancy dress and meet with paranormal investigators.

The Black Swan Hotel in Devizes, Wiltshire, dates back to 1737 and was once owned by alleged highwayman Ambrose Saintsbury.

It is said the present-day function room was once a court of judgement, and a meeting place for local freemasons and traders.

Guests who have stayed in room Number Four in the hotel report seeing a young woman in a dress sitting in a chair looking out of the window in the middle of the night.

Some paranormal investigators have also picked up abrupt temperature changes in the cellar and say this might be linked to hauntings.

But some experts say that what people are experiencing in the historic buildings is not true encounters with the paranormal.

Dr Joan Passey, a senior lecturer specialising in Gothic and horror literature at the University of Bristol, said people like to believe in ghost stories because it is "nicer than the alternative".

"We've had a concept of ghosts as long as there has been human storytelling. It's to provide a vocabulary to speak about the afterlife," Passey said.

"The stories sometimes present as comforting and reassuring. Sometimes they manifest as a challenge to all this scientific rationality to show there's still unexplained things."

She added that ghost stories could also be a reminder of histories in communities.

"Especially in the case of places and pubs, it's about the past persevering," Passey said.

articles.title: Secret Dorset: How a potting shed became a broadcasting icon
articles.summary: Radio Solent's Steve Harris looks at the story behind presenter Jack Hargreaves' famous potting shed.
articles.body:
There was a time when Jack Hargreaves' rustic potting shed was famous.

In the 1960s and 1970s, Hargreaves presented TV show Out of Town, a successful weekly documentary about traditional country life.

He would sit in a mocked-up shed, built inside a television studio, instantly recognisable with his white beard, briar pipe and wax jacket.

Later episodes were filmed in his actual shed at his home in Belchalwell, Dorset, with the show regularly beating Coronation Street in the ratings across the south of England.

In the beginning, Hargreaves would talk to the camera from inside the mock-up version at Southern TV's Northam studios in Southampton, Hampshire.

"[He] introduced films that he'd done and he talked over them," said cameraman Steve Wagstaff, who worked with the broadcaster.

"There was no sound on the films, it was just him talking around them live," he explained.

Born in London in 1911, Hargreaves produced morale-boosting public information broadcasts during World War Two.

He also ran political PR campaigns in the 1950s and, as deputy programme controller of Southern Television, even created long-running ITV educational children's TV programme How.

But his true love was the natural world.

"Sometimes we'd go out and film sheep shearing or meet blacksmiths or wheelwrights," said Wagstaff.

In 1982, Southern TV was taken over by Television South (TVS) and Hargreaves had to jump ship.

"The problem for Jack was he was part of the management team so he couldn't continue with TVS," the cameraman said.

"At the time, Channel Four was just starting and he decided to do the same programme but called Old Country for Channel Four."

For this new venture, Hargreaves' garden shed studio was set up inside the village hall in Meonstoke.

More than a decade later, the iconic set up was replicated in BBC comedy sketch series The Fast Show.

Charlie Higson played a genial countryside TV presenter character called Bob Fleming, who was to all intents and purposes Hargreaves, with a very bad cough.

Old Country lasted for three series and Hargreaves then entered the home video market.

He produced a series of 28 programmes under the original title Out of Town and, for these, Jack did his bits to camera from his actual shed at his home in Dorset.

"He moved to Belchalwell and he had a barn built in the back field," said Wagstaff.

"All the films that Southern TV had made were kept in storage. Those films were useless to anybody else so he acquired them.

"We went along to his real shed and we filmed the links between those films. He would present to camera and talk a bit about some aspect that was in the shed and then introduce the films."

In 1972, Hargreaves was awarded an OBE for his work on the Nugent Report, which looked how land owned by the Ministry of Defence could be returned to public or agricultural use.

The broadcaster died in Dorchester in 1994 and his ashes were reportedly scattered on Bulbarrow hill, just south of his Belchalwell home.

"The shed is still there," he said. "I went back there when the house changed hands and the shed has not been touched, it was the same as it was when we were filming there."

articles.title: Fugitive fraudster Arif Patel from Preston stole £33m from public
articles.summary: Arif Patel "should not be beyond the reach of the justice system," says the PM’s anti-corruption champion.
articles.body:
One of the UK's most prolific fraudsters, described by a judge as a "breathtakingly arrogant" and "totally dishonest" man, remains on the run in Dubai after stealing more than £33m of public money.

Arif Patel, from Preston in Lancashire, was exposed following a complex investigation spanning years, led by His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC), which established that he had tried to steal as much as £90m.

Patel, who skipped the UK in 2011 never to return, was eventually convicted in his absence and in 2023 was handed a 20-year prison sentence .

BBC File on 4 Investigates has been on the trail of the man who stole from all of us - and seemingly got away with it.

The fugitive fraudster who stole from you

"Al Capone was brought down by the taxman. This is the same situation and 20 years was more than a satisfying result," said Rod Stone, a veteran investigator of large-scale tax fraud, of Patel's conviction and custodial sentence.

The judge at Patel's sentencing hearing described him as the leader of a "fraternal organised crime group" with his brothers Munaf and Faisal who were "truly high-level criminals".

The fact that Arif Patel has not served a single day of his 20-year prison sentence clearly rankles with Stone.

For him and the dozens of others who were involved in bringing Patel down, there remains a strong sense that justice has only been served on paper.

In the early part of the millennium, Arif Patel appeared to be a businessman very much on the up.

His company, Faisaltex, headquartered in his home city of Preston, was known for manufacturing textiles, such as socks and nighties, which it supplied to retailers.

Patel was a fixture in the Sunday Times Rich List with his wealth in 2006 estimated to be £105m. He was also investing heavily in property across the city and beyond.

In 2007, his teenage son bought a minority stake in Preston North End Football Club. There was even a plan to build a £100m, 19-storey tower block - complete with botanical gardens and restaurant - in the centre of the city.

Behind the facade, though, something very different was going on.

In the early 2000s, organised crime groups had turned to large-scale attacks on the tax system through what became known as carousel fraud.

Chains of fake business transactions are created as a way of stealing VAT repayments from HMRC.

Goods move between different companies, into and out of the country, to generate false tax refunds.

The same shipments of goods are often moved around repeatedly, hence the name carousel fraud.

This type of fraud was costing taxpayers billions of pounds a year and experts like Stone were at the vanguard of the fightback.

This is how Patel's textiles empire appeared on his radar.

"When we started to look at them we did notice some very strange shipments of goods - a container load of hats to Switzerland seemed odd because they were actually Swiss hats," he said.

Most carousel fraudsters dealt in high-value, high-volume items like mobile phones or computer chips, for which investigators were on the lookout.

But Patel's enterprise had predominantly been dealing in textiles, making the scam harder to spot.

The team of investigators discovered Patel had successfully stolen more than £33m of taxpayers' money before HMRC cottoned on to what he was doing.

In total, he tried to steal more than £90m of public money - the rest of the payments were stopped.

Teams of investigators spent years working through vast chains of transactions until they were ready to make their move.

Patel was charged with a range of offences including conspiracies to cheat the taxman, money-laundering, false accounting and selling counterfeit goods.

But when he appeared at Bolton Crown Court in 2011, Patel asked the judge for permission to travel to Dubai on bail.

The judge agreed to this request and Patel left the UK, never to return.

In Dubai, he joined his brothers Munaf and Faisal, who had already left the country before they could be charged for their part in the conspiracy.

Over the next three years, 24 members of Patel's gang were convicted. Collectively, they were jailed for more than 116 years.

Efforts to have Arif Patel extradited back to the UK failed and he remained a free man in Dubai.

The BBC has heard claims he had been actively seeking to strike a deal with the UK authorities to settle the case against him.

"In my opinion, he thought he was above justice," said Graham Honey, another former HMRC investigator.

In 2020, he was working in the private sector when he said he was approached by Patel's representatives.

Honey said he was asked to open up a channel of communication with HMRC and the Crown Prosecution Service because Patel wanted to make a deal.

It soon became clear, however, that there would be a sticking point.

"It started to become apparent to me that Patel was not willing to come back," said Honey.

"He just thought he could get an agreement, pay some money, and this would all go away."

Honey claimed that while Patel was willing to admit his guilt and repay money, he was not prepared to face a criminal trial or the prospect of time behind bars.

He claimed it was not the first time that Patel had attempted to strike such a deal.

Honey said: "One of the officers told me that he had said 'I'm a tiger, not a caged tiger' meaning he was a big man, he'd done what he'd done, but in essence, he wasn't prepared to go to prison for it."

In 2023, Patel's trial got under way without him, something which is highly unusual and only done as a last resort.

He was found guilty of leading one of the UK's biggest carousel fraud gangs and received a 20-year jail sentence.

In 2025, he was subjected to a confiscation order to repay £90.5m through the sale of assets found to have been gained through criminality.

The funds raised were to be returned to the public purse.

But more than a year later, none of the money has been recouped because, despite being on the run overseas, Patel has been able to go to the Court of Appeal to object to the confiscation order.

So where is Patel now and what might he have done with his stolen millions?

The BBC has discovered that over the last few years, an increasing number of websites, press releases and social videos have begun to appear, celebrating the achievements of a businessman called Arif Patel in Dubai.

This Arif Patel is variously a business owner, an investor and a philanthropist. The photographs on the sites are often stock images or, in at least one case, belong to a different British entrepreneur.

Many of the pages also suggest Patel has links to Preston and worked in the textile industry.

A story was published in 2024 in which Arif Patel denies allegations of fraud by HMRC.

The article quotes a "Sam Mackenzie", who it said was a close associate of Patel.

Mackenzie spoke out in support of Patel, whom he described as a "pillar of integrity".

The piece also said he had received backing from an "Andrew Fox", who the article described as having reviewed the claims and deemed them to be "unfounded".

It just so happens that the deputy chief constable of Lancashire police is called Sam Mackenzie, while Andrew Fox is a senior prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service.

Their names appeared in other stories too, including one which claimed Patel had made a sizeable investment in HMRC anti-fraud technology in Lancashire.

The BBC does not know for certain whether Patel is connected to these sites, but File on 4 Investigates has established some sites are linked to an online reputation management company based in Dubai.

Another story was published earlier this year, this time about a donation Patel had made to a charitable organisation which supports children with disabilities in Dubai.

It shared similarities with some of the other websites but had one key difference - it featured a genuine photograph of Patel.

With an up-to-date picture, facial recognition technology uncovered numerous other pictures of Patel posing at glamorous events in Dubai.

We showed everything we had learned about the case to the prime minister's anti-corruption champion Dame Margaret Hodge.

"I think this is a shocking story of somebody who deliberately acted fraudulently and laundered money and he should be punished," she said.

"He should not be beyond the reach of the British justice system.

"I think he is clearly abusing the justice system in a way that only rich people can.

"There's an intrinsic injustice in a system that allows those with money to delay the implementation of a punishment for a crime and to delay the confiscation of assets which was stolen as part of that crime."

The BBC contacted the Government of Dubai but did not receive a response.

The BBC also contacted Arif Patel via his Manchester-based solicitor - as well as his brothers Munaf and Faisal - but did not hear back.

articles.title: Nebraska workers cut 150 trees from crowded lake banks and sank them at 16 underwater locations; the September 2026 project is building shelter for young fish in two lakes without using concrete reefs
articles.summary: Instead of building concrete reefs, conservation workers in Nebraska have turned trees cleared from overgrown lake banks into underwater fish habitats,
articles.body: Instead of building concrete reefs, conservation workers in Nebraska have turned trees cleared from overgrown lake banks into underwater fish habitats, placing around 150 trees at 16 locations across two lakes. The project, completed in September 2026, aims to give smaller fish places to hide from predators while improving fishing access along the shore. According to the Nebraska Game and Parks Commission, the trees were transported and submerged using a new Aquatic Habitat Barge at Bridgeport State Recreation Area.The project used approximately 60 cedar and Russian olive trees at five locations in the recreation area's southeast lake and another 90 trees at 11 locations in the middle lake. The trees were removed from crowded shoreline areas, allowing crews to address two problems at once: overgrown banks that restricted access for anglers and a shortage of underwater woody habitat for fish.The commission announced the work on October 22, explaining that the brush piles would provide shelter for smaller fish and help support the aquatic food web. The project is part of Nebraska's wider effort to improve lake habitats and make fishing more productive.How trees become underwater fish sheltersTrees that might otherwise be removed as shoreline vegetation can serve another purpose once submerged. Their branches and trunks create a network of spaces where small fish can hide, making it harder for larger predatory fish to reach them. The underwater structures also provide surfaces where algae and other organisms can grow. These can attract plankton and small aquatic creatures, which in turn become food for fish. The resulting chain of interactions helps support a wider aquatic food web.The Nebraska Game and Parks Commission said the brush piles are intended to benefit fish populations and anglers by improving habitat conditions. However, the announcement does not provide post-project monitoring data demonstrating a measured increase in fish numbers at the two lakes. The trees are not simply dumped into the water at random. Crews transport and position them at selected underwater locations, while the commission makes approximate placement information available through its lake habitat and structure maps. These help anglers identify underwater features that may attract fish.The project also illustrates how vegetation removed for one practical reason can be reused to address a different environmental need.Clearing crowded banks improves fishing accessThe work has a benefit beyond the underwater ecosystem. The cedar and Russian olive trees were cut from overgrown shoreline areas, opening up sections of the banks for anglers. Shoreline vegetation can restrict access to the water, particularly at locations where trees and branches have grown densely. Removing selected trees can make it easier for people to reach the water's edge while allowing some of the same material to be reused as fish habitat.Bridgeport State Recreation Area, located in western Nebraska, covers approximately 326 acres, including 78 acres of water spread across five sandpit lakes. The area offers fishing, boating, camping, swimming and other outdoor activities, according to the state agency. Its waters support several fish species, including largemouth bass, walleye, bluegill, yellow perch and channel catfish. Rainbow trout are also stocked in some of the area's lakes. Improving underwater habitat can help fisheries managers maintain suitable conditions for fish while making recreational waters more useful to visitors.Part of a wider habitat restoration effortNebraska has been using a range of approaches to improve aquatic habitats, including submerged trees, artificial fish attractors and rock structures. The Nebraska Game and Parks Commission's Aquatic Habitat Program was established in 1997. According to the agency, it has generated more than $90 million for improvements to 137 water bodies across the state. The programme supports projects intended to improve aquatic conditions, fisheries and recreational access.A 2026 overview published by Nebraskaland Magazine, the commission's outdoor publication, describes other efforts involving woody habitat. At 11 lakes along Interstate 80, invasive eastern red cedar and Russian olive trees were removed to improve shoreline access, with some of the cut trees placed in the lakes to create fish habitat.The state has also used rock shoals at other reservoirs. In partnership with the US Bureau of Reclamation, 42 shoals were built at Medicine Creek Reservoir in 2025, following the construction of 43 at Swanson Reservoir in 2023. These structures provide underwater habitat in areas that otherwise offer relatively few features for fish.The different projects show that habitat restoration does not depend on a single design. Depending on the water body and its needs, managers can use woody material, rocks or purpose-built structures to increase habitat diversity. The Bridgeport project specifically uses trees rather than newly constructed rock structures. However, the commission has not described it as a formal replacement for concrete reefs, and the wider state programme continues to use other habitat-building methods where appropriate.Can the new habitat help fish populations?The immediate objective is to create places where smaller fish can escape predators and where food organisms can gather. Such structures can make underwater environments more complex, providing fish with shelter and feeding opportunities that may be scarce in open areas.The commission expects the improved habitat to support healthier fish populations and better fishing opportunities. Whether the new brush piles produce a measurable increase in fish abundance at Bridgeport will depend on factors including water conditions, food availability, predation and the long-term use of the structures by different species.The state has made the approximate locations of the newly installed brush piles available through its lake contour and habitat maps, allowing anglers to find the underwater structures.For now, the September project offers a practical example of how clearing overgrown shorelines can do more than improve access. By placing the cut trees beneath the water, Nebraska's fisheries managers have converted vegetation into a resource intended to support fish, aquatic food webs and recreational fishing.You use AI every day. articles.title: Urad dal, roti and 6am wake-up call: Influencer-model Shraddha Dubey adjusts to life inside Lucknow jail
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: Shraddha Dubey, the prime accused in the murder of Lucknow restaurateur Shiva Sharma, and her sister Rashmi Dubey have been moved to the general
articles.body: LUCKNOW: Shraddha Dubey, the prime accused in the murder of Lucknow restaurateur Shiva Sharma, and her sister Rashmi Dubey have been moved to the general women's barrack at Gosai Ganj District Jail after completing their quarantine period. The sisters, who were reportedly used to a lavish lifestyle, are now adjusting to the prison's strict routine and regular meals.The two were lodged in jail on Thursday and shifted to a barrack housing 45 female inmates on Friday. According to the jail administration, Shraddha appeared tense when she arrived on Thursday night and could not finish her first meal, which included whole urad dal, roti and potato-soy fenugreek curry.The sisters reportedly had a restless night and were woken up at 6am on Friday as per jail rules. They were served sweet porridge and tea for breakfast, followed by whole urad dal, rajma, potato-bottle gourd curry, rice and roti for lunch. Dinner comprised arhar dal, potato-pumpkin curry and roti. Jail officials said the sisters were receiving the same food as other inmates.Neither sister received a visit from relatives on Friday. They reportedly remained quiet in the barrack throughout the day and did not interact with other inmates, although they were occasionally seen talking to each other. Jail officials said they were gradually getting used to the prison environment.District Jail Jailer Ritwik Priyadarshi said Shraddha, Rashmi and their driver, Tanveer alias Danish, had been moved to regular barracks after completing quarantine. A female deputy jailer is monitoring the sisters, while a male deputy jailer is supervising Tanveer. For security reasons, all three will appear before the court through video conferencing on their scheduled judicial custody dates.Meanwhile, investigators are looking into the alleged role of people who may have helped the accused after Sharma's death. Police found that Rashmi had allegedly called a man named Aamir for help shortly after Sharma fell from the building. CCTV footage obtained from the hospital reportedly shows Aamir Sheikh, wearing a black T-shirt, with Tanveer alias Danish. Police teams are now searching for those suspected of helping the accused.How police traced the accused to NagpurShraddha, Rashmi and Danish were arrested in Nagpur on October 20 after Lucknow Police tracked their movements through WhatsApp calls, internet connection details and information provided by a cab driver.Investigators said the trio had repeatedly changed locations to evade arrest. The frequent moves made it difficult for police to catch up with them, as internet connection details used for surveillance took around 14 to 15 hours to reach investigators, leaving the teams nearly three hours behind the suspects.Police said the accused allegedly stayed at each location for less than 12 hours before moving elsewhere to avoid detection. The investigation gained momentum after officers traced and questioned a cab driver who had taken the trio to Nagpur.According to investigators, Shraddha mainly used her driver Danish's mobile phone for WhatsApp calls. During the journey, she allegedly accessed the internet through a hotspot provided by the cab driver.The driver dropped the trio in Nagpur late on October 19 and waited outside a hotel for another passenger travelling to Kanpur. Police traced him and questioned him, and the information he provided helped narrow the search.A Lucknow Police team then reached Nagpur and increased surveillance, waiting for another WhatsApp call that could reveal the suspects' location. Shraddha allegedly made a call that helped investigators trace the signal to a flat in the Pro-Zone Calm apartment complex in Chinchbhan.When officers reached the flat on the afternoon of October 20, the occupants allegedly refused to open the door. Police sought assistance from Nagpur Police, after which the door was opened and the three were arrested.They were subsequently brought back to Lucknow. Police had announced a reward of Rs 50,000 each for information leading to their arrest.Sharma died on October 9 after falling from the fourth floor of an apartment near Balu Adda in Lucknow's Hazratganj area. articles.title: Keeping the world safe when no one is in charge
articles.summary: As AI creates new threats and power becomes fragmented, international cooperation is more vital than ever.
articles.body:
International politics today feels like a collective sleepwalk into the abyss. Three trends are particularly alarming. Artificial intelligence is globalising and turbocharging old and new threats. Meanwhile, no state is strong enough to impose order. And, as in earlier periods of global crisis, geopolitical blocs are hardening, with international cooperation increasingly portrayed as weakness. Alas, there is ample reason to fear a repetition of the worst of history.

Much attention has focused on the risk of war between the US and China, as shifts in hegemonic power historically produce conflict. That is not, however, what is happening. Instead, we are approaching an international order with no hegemon, with several states and regional blocs competing for influence. Using the jargon of international relations theory, we are on the cusp of genuine global multipolarity.

Artificial intelligence is adding further stress to existing power structures. On the one hand, we are all being transformed into godlike figures — soon no innovation or information is beyond our reach. But it is also disempowering everyone, creating new threats and making old ones harder to contain.

Larger states are finding it increasingly difficult to convert power into control. This is already evident in the military domain, where inexpensive drones and AI-assisted targeting have changed traditional hierarchies. The US, with its vast military arsenal, is unable to force an isolated and bankrupt theocracy in Iran to bend the knee; Russia’s failed attempt at subjugating Ukraine is another example of a much more powerful state not getting its way.

New technology is making the loss of control even more evident in other domains. The next pandemic could originate in a hidden laboratory and prove far deadlier than COVID-19. Devastating cyberattacks could be launched from someone’s garage. Frontier AI systems could spiral beyond human control. AI could lower the barriers to developing nuclear weapons, while biological weapons could proliferate without anyone noticing.

Such threats recognise no borders. If one state establishes effective safety measures, nefarious actors will simply move somewhere else and deploy from there. A state can possess overwhelming military and economic capabilities and still be unable to stop a pathogen, prevent a cyberattack or contain the spread of dangerous technologies. Strategies based on peace through strength, regional primacy and zero-sum power dynamics will be like fighting mosquitoes with heavy weaponry — costly and unworkable.

Yet much of the world is doubling down on precisely these strategies. Some state leaders are focusing on winning AI and achieving digital supremacy. Negotiating mutual constraints through international law and institutions is seen as naive or self-defeating. Such approaches are at best ineffective. As global policy, they can destroy humanity. It is as though one can hear the voices of earlier wartime generations: “Do not fall for it again.”

And we really shouldn’t, given how unfettered national ambition coupled with weak international rules and institutions has hurt us in the past. Yet many seem incapable of rising to the occasion. One reason is surely our tendency to underestimate risks that accumulate over time. A 1 percent annual probability of a global catastrophe may sound reassuringly small. Yet, over a century that translates into roughly a 63 percent chance of catastrophe—an intolerable level of risk.

Military strength will remain necessary. But the only way to ensure real security in this new paradigm of multipolarity and artificial intelligence is through powerful international institutions and laws. Global standards must be developed and enforced. International organisations must be allowed to monitor, inspect and report on activities within countries’ borders. Governments will regularly have to share sensitive information. Peace through cooperation must be the new global slogan; not out of altruism but because it is the only way to achieve real security.

Fortunately, we don’t have to start from scratch. Institutions such as the United Nations, the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the World Health Organization (WHO) still retain unparalleled authority and legitimacy. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has shown that international monitoring can effectively verify compliance even in highly sensitive areas.

Recent events offer some grounds for optimism. Last year, the WHO adopted a Pandemic Agreement, which will improve the world’s collective readiness to prevent and mitigate future health emergencies. The UN General Assembly recently adopted the BBNJ Agreement to protect biodiversity on the high seas, the first global treaty of consequence in at least a decade. The Security Council has shown that it’s serious about addressing the security challenges posed by AI; during a high-profile debate in September this year, most governments and leading AI developers alike called for stronger global governance and more robust international oversight mechanisms.

These are encouraging signs. But overall, states are investing too little in such global frameworks at a time when the opposite is needed.

Norway has made it a priority to break the curve. We have defined respect for international law and effective multilateral institutions as a core national security interest. We’re investing heavily in UN reform; as one of the UN’s largest financial contributors, we have leverage which we will use to push for greater effectiveness. Alone, Norway is too small to change the course of international politics. But through cross-regional coalitions with like-minded countries, we can make a real difference.

One recent example came in September when Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb launched a joint Call for Action to establish global oversight and control over advanced AI models. Countries from all over the globe have joined the initiative. Hopefully, it can serve as a springboard for concrete international action in this field.

No one is in charge in a multipolar world. This new reality is taking shape precisely as technology is making threats harder to contain. The defining challenge of our time will therefore be to couple multipolarity with multilateralism. Building effective institutions when no one can impose order is inherently difficult. But just as previous generations were able to overcome profound challenges, so can we.

It was only after the lived catastrophes of the first and second World Wars that nations united around shared legal principles and institutions. I am convinced that, in time, states will once again realise that this is the only way. What remains to be seen, however, is whether we can muster the necessary resolve without first experiencing another global crisis of world-war-like proportions.

articles.title: COP17 puts Armenia’s environmental record in the spotlight
articles.summary: As Yerevan hosts the global biodiversity summit, concerns over mining and environmental protection deserve scrutiny.
articles.body:
Last weekend, the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) opened in Yerevan with a lavish ceremony. It is the first time the summit has been hosted by a former Soviet republic, an occasion the Armenian government has celebrated as an opportunity to establish the country as a leader in environmental protection. But Armenia’s own ecological record raises serious questions about its suitability for this role.

When Yerevan was awarded the right to host COP17 in 2024, the Armenian authorities celebrated the decision as recognition of the country’s environmental ambitions. Yet Armenia has struggled for decades to develop effective conservation policies, and its record remains poor in several important areas. In Yale University’s 2026 Environmental Performance Index , Armenia ranks 75th out of 177 countries, compared with first place for Estonia, another former Soviet republic.

Its performance is particularly poor on waste management, where it ranks 164th, and wastewater treatment, where it ranks 165th. These figures point to serious shortcomings in basic environmental protection.

The contrast raises an obvious question: why was a country facing such serious environmental challenges chosen to host one of the world’s most important biodiversity conferences? The selection might have offered an opportunity to encourage change, but there is little indication that the Armenian authorities have used the occasion to address the country’s longstanding problems.

A major obstacle is the structure of Armenia’s economy, in which mining plays an important role, alongside ageing industrial facilities and inadequate environmental regulation. The country’s largest mining operations, including the Zangezur, Agarak and Teghut copper-molybdenum mines, extract ore using open-pit methods that generate large quantities of waste and pose serious pollution risks. The World Bank has identified mining as a significant source of environmental pollution in Armenia. Open-pit gold mining has also been licensed at Meghrasar, on land that originally overlapped with Arevik National Park, before the government reduced the park’s boundaries in 2015. The Artsvanik tailings reservoir, which holds millions of tonnes of mining waste, has also been linked to heavy-metal contamination in nearby waterways.

Armenia’s environmental problems extend beyond mining. Forests cover only 11.1 percent of the country, while in Yerevan, levels of harmful fine particle air pollution are about five times the World Health Organization’s recommended limit.

Armenia’s dependence on Russian-linked businesses in some of its most important industrial sectors further complicates efforts to strengthen environmental regulation. These companies are not only major investors and employers, but also important contributors to the state budget, giving the government a powerful economic incentive to protect their operations. Russian-linked investors hold a controlling stake in the Zangezur copper-molybdenum complex, which was Armenia’s largest taxpayer in the first half of 2026.

That conflict between economic interests and environmental protection was on display just days before COP17, when Armenia inaugurated the controversial Amulsar gold mine. Environmental organisations, including the Global Forest Coalition and various Armenian civil society groups, have condemned the move, arguing that it disregards longstanding environmental concerns and recommendations under the Bern Convention.

Human rights organisations have documented intimidation and lawsuits targeting activists campaigning against Amulsar. Armenia’s Economy Minister has defended the project on economic grounds, saying it could contribute between 1.5 and 2 percent of the country’s GDP and generate approximately $130m annually in taxes and other payments to the state budget. The projected revenues expose the contradiction between the government’s determination to expand mining and its ambition to present Armenia as an international leader in biodiversity protection.

These competing priorities are particularly important as Armenia seeks closer relations with the European Union and distances itself from Moscow. The EU–Armenia Strategic Agenda identifies the need for stronger implementation of environmental impact assessment legislation, improvements to waste management, and further action on air quality, water protection and industrial emissions. Progress on these commitments should be central to the EU’s assessment of Armenia’s efforts towards closer integration.

At COP17, governments are reviewing progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which aims to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030. The summit is expected to finalise a “Yerevan Pathway” to accelerate implementation of its targets. The prospects are already bleak. The State of Biodiversity Action report , launched before the summit, found that fewer than half of assessed national targets are on track.

Financing remains a major obstacle. Developed countries have provided about $16bn annually in international biodiversity finance, falling short of the $20bn target for 2025. Meanwhile, the Cali Fund, established with the goal of collecting $1bn in annual contributions from companies profiting from genetic data derived from nature, has received just $6,000. These shortfalls illustrate the difficulties facing governments as they seek to turn their biodiversity commitments into action.

As host of COP17, Armenia should be prepared to demonstrate that the commitments being discussed in Yerevan also apply to its own mining industry, environmental regulations and treatment of conservation activists. Participating governments should use the summit to press the Armenian authorities to strengthen environmental protections, enforce pollution controls, ensure credible environmental impact assessments and address the concerns raised by civil society over projects such as Amulsar.

articles.title: Displaced West Bank Palestinians face growing hunger after UN cuts food aid
articles.summary: Already struggling after losing homes to Israeli military operations, Palestinians face hardship as WFP halves aid.
articles.body:
Tulkarem, occupied West Bank – Fawza Awad, a 75-year-old widow, couldn’t hold back her tears as she described the living conditions she has endured since being displaced from the Tulkarem refugee camp in January 2025 – a result of an Israeli military operation that targeted refugee camps in the northern West Bank, forcibly displacing tens of thousands of Palestinians from their homes.

With little money, Fawza and her family found shelter where they could: a small, unfinished house in Tulkarem belonging to her daughter. She currently lives in a portion of the structure alongside her son, his wife, and their child.

The family previously relied on limited financial and food assistance provided by the World Food Programme (WFP), but has not received aid in the past five months.

The UN agency officially announced a 50 percent reduction in the number of food aid recipients in the occupied West Bank in September, citing “critical funding constraints”, the result of reduced funding from international funders. Food needs, conversely, have more than doubled since 2023, when Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza, and increased attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank.

The WFP noted at the time that approximately 900,000 people in the West Bank are currently suffering from food insecurity.

In a statement given to Al Jazeera, the WFP confirmed that some families had stopped receiving aid before the official announcement in September.

Fawza and her family have been left to fend for themselves. There is no prospect of returning to her old home – she says that the Israeli army has completely demolished the structure, replacing it with a wide road to facilitate the movement of its military vehicles.

She added that one of her sons has been detained by Israel since 2024, while her other sons, who previously worked inside Israel, are now all unemployed.

“I suffer from asthma and high blood pressure, requiring monthly medication that costs at least 200 shekels ($64), an expense no one covers for me. We used to receive modest food aid barely enough for two or three people, but now that has stopped completely,” Fawza told Al Jazeera.

Not far away, in the al-Muwahhad School building in the Thannabeh suburb of Tulkarem, more than 1,000 Palestinians displaced from the Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps are sheltering, having found nowhere else to go and unable to pay rent.

Among them are Rabab Qasim, 47, her husband Talib Abu Sarriya, 72, and their three children. For the second consecutive year, they have been living in a small, 30-square-metre (320sq-foot) room on the ground floor of the school, with no source of income and totally reliant on aid.

For the past three months, the family has received no aid whatsoever following the WFP food assistance cut.

“I suffer from a herniated disc in my back, requiring monthly treatment that costs 300 shekels ($96) – an amount I cannot afford,” Rabab said. “I also need physical therapy, which I have never been able to access because I cannot pay for it. I sleep on a worn-out mattress on the floor; all I wish for is to be able to buy a bed.”

Talib told Al Jazeera that the family are often unable to find bread or a meal, and frequently go to sleep hungry. It’s a far cry from their former life in the Tulkarem refugee camp, where he once owned a small vegetable stall. It was a modest livelihood, but one that gave them enough to get by.

The WFP has blamed increasing Israeli pogroms and forced displacements in the West Bank for devastating livelihoods, deepening hunger, and pushing families into even more severe crises. The latest quarterly food security analysis conducted by the WFP indicates that 76 percent of Palestinian households in the West Bank have experienced a significant decline in income.

According to the analysis, 12 percent of the population has poor food consumption, and one-third of households cannot afford a healthy diet due to rapidly deteriorating economic conditions. Rural areas and the governorates in the southern occupied West Bank have been the hardest hit.

Said al-Amour, 61, a resident of Khirbet al-Rakeez in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, told Al Jazeera that he and his 14-person family haven’t received any assistance from the WFP for the past seven months.

In April 2025, while confronting repeated attacks by settlers on the village, Said says he was shot by a settler. The injury resulted in the amputation of his leg and a permanent disability; he continues to face periodic assaults and beatings whenever he encounters the settlers – part of the ongoing pogrom against Palestinians in the West Bank.

“They are trying to steal our land. I refuse to let them take it, and I will continue to defend it, but I am paying a heavy price. Now, they have cut off the aid I used to receive that helped my family remain steadfast here,” he told Al Jazeera.

Due to the amputation of his leg, al-Amour requires monthly medical treatment costing at least 1,200 shekels ($385), an expense that he cannot afford. He has no source of income other than a few olive trees, which settlers frequently attempt to seize.

In cooperation with its partners, the WFP still provides assistance to 200,000 Palestinians in the West Bank through cash transfers, food vouchers, direct food supplies, livelihood programmes, and nutritional services.

However, the WFP told Al Jazeera that it simply does not have the resources to cover the needs of all the families in the West Bank requiring assistance.

“The cessation of aid does not imply that a beneficiary is ineligible; rather, it is a broad decision affecting all current beneficiaries, regardless of the outcome of their individual assessment,” the WFP said. “It is possible that changes may occur, and aid could be reinstated for some beneficiaries; in such cases, they would be contacted and notified via text message.”

Economist and human rights activist Ubai Aboudi told Al Jazeera that the West Bank is facing a humanitarian crisis exacerbated by the loss of the WFP food aid, as well as a financial crisis affecting the Palestinian Authority (PA). Israel has completely withheld the customs revenues it collects on behalf of the PA since May 2025, leaving the authority unable to pay public sector salaries.

Aboudi noted other factors, such as the tens of thousands of Palestinians previously employed in Israel and illegal settlements in the West Bank who have been out of work since October 2023, when Israel stopped giving them work permits.

He also added that Israeli restrictions on Palestinian and international NGOs, including the suspension of registration for 37 international organisations and the closure of some local groups, have further limited the ability to provide humanitarian assistance.

“Around half a million Palestinian families need food assistance, while the actual need may be greater,” Aboudi said. “With aid declining from the World Food Programme and other sources, many families are unable to secure food.”

articles.title: A 2019 flood raised an Antarctic lake by 2 metres after water escaped from a neighbouring glacier-fed lake; scientists traced its effects on carbon cycling and microbial life
articles.summary: In January 2019, a rare glacial flood caused an Antarctic lake to rise by two metres after a neighbouring lake released 17.5 million cubic metres of water.
articles.body: In January 2019, a rare glacial flood caused an Antarctic lake to rise by two metres after a neighbouring lake released 17.5 million cubic metres of water. The event transformed Lake Untersee’s water chemistry and prompted scientists to investigate its effects on an unusual microbial ecosystem living beneath its permanent ice cover. The study, published in ResearchGate and titled ‘Glacial lake outburst floods enhance benthic microbial productivity in perennially ice-covered Lake Untersee (East Antarctica)', found that the flood altered carbon concentrations and other chemical properties, potentially supporting photosynthetic microbial activity. Researchers also analysed microbial mats for evidence of earlier flooding, finding indications that similar events may have periodically influenced the lake’s carbon cycling over thousands of years.How the 2019 Antarctic Lake flood changed microbial lifeThe flood began on 14–15 January 2019, when water was suddenly released through the ice cover of Lake Obersee. The researchers reported that the water travelled approximately 8.3 kilometres through a narrow channel along the eastern lateral moraine before entering the north-eastern corner of Lake Untersee. The event followed a decrease of 11.3 metres in Lake Obersee’s water level.According to the researchers, the flood added 17.5 million cubic metres of water to Lake Untersee, increasing its volume by three per cent. Lake Obersee experienced a volume decrease of 22.9 million cubic metres, suggesting that some of the released water may have drained towards the coast rather than entering Lake Untersee. The study estimated the flood’s average discharge at approximately nine to ten cubic metres per second over 21 days. The researchers also documented thermal erosion of the Anuchin Glacier and the adjacent moraine, along with the formation of a melt pool approximately 50 metres wide where the incoming water entered Lake Untersee.Lake Untersee’s unique microbial ecosystem before the 2019 floodLake Untersee is one of the large, permanently ice-covered lakes in the Untersee Oasis of Dronning Maud Land, East Antarctica. It is approximately 6.5 kilometres long and 2.5 kilometres wide, with a maximum depth of 169 metres. Its water chemistry is unusual, with a high pH of around 10.6 and extremely low concentrations of dissolved inorganic and organic carbon. Before the 2019 flood, the lake had remained in a state of hydrological stability for several hundred years, according to the study.Despite the low availability of nutrients and the limited light penetrating its thick ice cover, Lake Untersee supports a benthic microbial ecosystem. The researchers described photosynthetic microbial mats, small pinnacles and large conical structures resembling stromatolites on the lake bed. Cyanobacteria, including Tychonema, Phormidium, Leptolyngbya and Pseudanabaena, dominate the upper layer of the mats, where photosynthesis fixes carbon. The underlying layers contain heterotrophic microorganisms, including members of the Actinobacteria, Verrucomicrobia, Proteobacteria and Bacteroidetes groups.How the 2019 flood changed Lake Untersee’s water chemistryThe researchers found that the flood altered the chemical composition of Lake Untersee’s oxygenated water column. The lake’s pH decreased from 10.5 to 9.5, while specific conductivity fell from between 505 and 520 microsiemens per centimetre to 485 microsiemens per centimetre. Dissolved oxygen also decreased, from 150 per cent to 128 per cent saturation.The concentration of total inorganic carbon increased from 0.35 milligrams of carbon per litre to 0.5 milligrams per litre. The researchers also recorded changes in carbon isotope measurements, which helped them investigate the origin of the additional carbon. When the team returned to the lake in November 2019, a small stream was still flowing through the flood channel into its north-eastern corner. The stream had a pH of 7.7 and a total inorganic carbon concentration of 1.8 milligrams per litre, considerably different from the lake’s usual high-pH, low-carbon conditions.How the 2019 flood affected carbon availability in Lake UnterseeThe researchers explained that the lake’s photosynthetic microbial mats operate under conditions of extremely limited carbon availability. Before the flood, the uppermost layer of the mats was understood to be carbon dioxide-depleted, restricting photosynthesis and the sequestration of organic carbon.The flood may have supplied additional carbon to the lake, helping to support phototrophic activity. The researchers attributed the higher concentrations of total inorganic carbon and modern carbon recorded after the event partly to the uptake of atmospheric carbon dioxide through the melt pool that formed near the flood’s entry point. They estimated that an additional uptake of 0.11 milligrams of carbon per litre, equivalent to 21 per cent of the measured total inorganic carbon, would be required to account for both the post-flood carbon concentration and radiocarbon measurements.How ancient floods shaped Lake Untersee’s carbon storageThe researchers also investigated whether similar floods had occurred before 2019. They analysed the grain sizes and carbon isotopes of microbial mats, finding evidence consistent with periodic glacial lake outburst floods during the Holocene. These findings offered a possible explanation for some of the complex patterns of carbon cycling and sequestration observed in Lake Untersee.Lake Untersee stores between 5.42 billion and 6.71 billion grams of carbon, with more than 95 per cent of that carbon held in its microbial mats. The researchers concluded that periodic flooding could replenish carbon in lakes where carbon dioxide availability is limited, potentially supporting microbial productivity over long periods. They suggested that similar processes might be relevant to other carbon dioxide-depleted Antarctic ecosystems, while also discussing their possible relevance to icy lakes on early Mars.The 2019 event demonstrated that a lake that had remained stable for centuries could undergo a substantial hydrological and chemical change following the partial drainage of a neighbouring lake. By combining satellite observations, water chemistry measurements and analyses of microbial mats, the researchers documented how the flood changed Lake Untersee and investigated the role that such events may play in sustaining its unusual ecosystem.You use AI every day. articles.title: Jensen Ackles and his family bought a 15-acre Texas ranch and turned it into a destination brewery; six years after opening, the public taproom closed but its beers continued reaching stores across Texas
articles.summary: For Jensen Ackles, the idea of a family business was already part of his professional mythology.
articles.body: For Jensen Ackles, the idea of a family business was already part of his professional mythology. After years of playing Dean Winchester on Supernatural, where family, loyalty and adventure formed the heart of the story, the actor brought a version of that ethos into real life. In Dripping Springs, Texas, Ackles, his wife Danneel and brother-in-law Gino Graul transformed a 15-acre property into Family Business Beer Co., a destination built around craft beer, food, music and community. What began as a backyard experiment eventually became a full-fledged brewery, although its journey has since taken a different direction. Scroll down read the details.From backyard brews to a Texas destinationThe origins of Family Business Beer Co. were surprisingly informal. While living in California, Ackles and the Graul family began experimenting with a small brewing system that had been stored in the actor's backyard. Weekend brewing sessions gradually developed into a genuine passion, prompting Gino Graul to pursue formal brewing education, including studies at UC Davis and the Siebel Institute in Chicago, states a 2018 Forbes report.The family eventually brought the concept to Texas, where Ackles and Danneel had settled after moving to Austin in 2014. Construction on the Dripping Springs brewery began in 2017, turning their interest in craft beer into a substantial hospitality venture.According to Forbes, Ackles remained deeply involved in the project despite his demanding acting schedule, contributing to everything from design and construction details to testing the brewery's evolving selection of beers.More than just a breweryAccording to Yahoo, when Family Business Beer Co. opened in January 2018, it was designed as an experience rather than simply a place to grab a drink. articles.title: Iran trying harder to target US personnel in Middle East, intelligence chief warns
articles.summary: The warning comes as the US State Department makes adjustments to staffing at diplomatic posts in the region.
articles.body:
Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target US personnel" in the Middle East and other areas, the US national intelligence director has warned in a memo seen by the BBC.

Jay Clayton's assessment come as the US State Department makes adjustments to staffing at diplomatic posts in the region, including the ordered departure earlier this week of non-emergency US embassy staff from Saudi Arabia.

The order came in response to escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia in the past month.

Clayton's memo was marked unclassified and sent to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday.

It said: "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries."

Clayton said he was making every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so Rubio could share it with US State Department personnel.

A US official told the BBC: "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment.

"The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."

At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.

One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

The Houthis say the attacks on Saudi Arabia are in retaliation to what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport they blame on the kingdom.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks. Some 155 civilians have been killed in Yemen since, according to the Houthi-run health ministry.

This particular conflict has re-emerged on the backdrop of a wider conflict in the Middle East.

The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.

In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has seen oil prices surge, exacerbated by the Houthis' "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: Jeff Bezos’s parents invested $245,573 in Amazon when it was an uncertain online bookstore; that early family investment is worth billions today as the company’s valuation passes $2 trillion
articles.summary: When Jeff Bezos decided to leave his secure job in 1994 to build an online bookstore, he was pursuing an idea that many people struggled to understand.
articles.body: When Jeff Bezos decided to leave his secure job in 1994 to build an online bookstore, he was pursuing an idea that many people struggled to understand. The internet was still unfamiliar to most investors and the future of online shopping remained uncertain. His parents, Jackie and Mike Bezos, nevertheless backed him with $245,573 from their savings in 1995. Bezos later recalled that he warned them they could lose their money. They invested anyway because they believed in their son. Nearly three decades later, Amazon has grown from a small internet bookseller into a global technology and retail giant. The family's early decision has since become one of the most remarkable investment stories linked to the company's rise.Jeff Bezos’s parents’ risky bet on an unfamiliar businessThe idea for Amazon came to Bezos in 1994 while he was working at an investment firm in New York. He saw the rapid growth of the internet as an opportunity to create a bookstore with a catalogue far larger than any physical shop could accommodate.Bezos decided to leave his job and pursue the idea in Seattle. His parents provided most of the initial start-up capital, putting a substantial portion of their life savings into a business they did not fully understand.In his July 2020 testimony before the US House Judiciary Committee, Bezos said he had told his parents there was a 70% chance they would lose their investment. He explained that they were not necessarily betting on the concept of an online bookstore. They were betting on him.The decision came at a time when convincing investors to back an internet business was difficult. Bezos said he attended more than 50 meetings while trying to raise $1 million. One question repeatedly came up during those discussions: what was the internet?From a small online bookstore to a public companyAmazon opened its online store in 1995. The business initially focused on books because the internet offered a way to display a vast selection without the physical limitations of a traditional shop.The response surprised Bezos. In a later account of Amazon's early days, he recalled receiving orders from customers across all 50 US states and 45 countries soon after the store opened.Amazon went public in May 1997 at $18 per share. The initial public offering raised approximately $54 million and gave the company additional capital to expand its operations.Its future was far from secure, however. Amazon recorded cumulative losses of nearly $3 billion between its founding and the end of 2001. It did not report a profitable quarter until the final three months of that year.The company also faced scepticism during the dot-com bubble. Its share price reached $116 at the height of the internet boom before falling to $6 after the bubble burst. Bezos recalled that commentators questioned whether Amazon could survive.How the family's investment grewThe $245,573 investment came in Amazon’s early years, before the company went public. Mike Bezos bought 582,528 shares in February 1995, while Jackie Bezos bought another 847,716 shares in July that year.As Amazon grew from an online bookstore into a global retail and cloud computing giant, its share value increased significantly. The company’s growth turned the family’s early investment into a potentially enormous fortune.The family also donated some of its Amazon shares to the Bezos Family Foundation. According to a 2018 Los Angeles Times report, Jackie and Mike Bezos donated 595,027 shares to the foundation between 2001 and 2016.The exact value of the shares they still hold is not publicly known. A September 2026 Fortune report estimated that Mike Bezos’s remaining stake could be worth about $51.7 billion if he still holds the shares not accounted for by those donations. This is an estimate, not a confirmed figure.Amazon's growth transformed the original gambleAmazon's rise was not driven by online retail alone. Over time, it expanded into cloud computing, digital advertising, streaming, logistics and other technology services.One of its most consequential developments was Amazon Web Services. Bezos said in his congressional testimony that some observers initially viewed cloud computing as a distraction from the company's retail business. AWS eventually became a major part of Amazon's operations.The company also expanded its marketplace by allowing independent sellers to offer products alongside Amazon's own inventory. Bezos said third-party sellers accounted for approximately 60% of physical product sales on Amazon at the time of his 2020 testimony.The family continued to support education and young peopleJackie and Mike Bezos established the Bezos Family Foundation in 2000 with their children and their spouses. The foundation has focused largely on education and child development, supporting research and programmes designed to help young people.The family's donations of Amazon shares helped channel part of its wealth towards philanthropic work. The foundation's activities provide another dimension to the investment story, connecting the family's early financial support for Bezos with its later efforts to fund educational initiatives.A decision made before Amazon's success was clearThe story of the Bezos family's investment is striking because the outcome was not obvious when the money changed hands. In 1995, Amazon was a young business built around a new way of selling books. Its founder had left a secure job, investors were still learning about the internet and the company had years of financial challenges ahead.Jackie and Mike Bezos accepted the possibility of losing a substantial portion of their savings because they believed in their son. Amazon's eventual growth turned that decision into a landmark example of early backing for a successful technology company.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
