articles.title: Dan Sullivan vs Dan Sullivan: Why is Trump’s DOJ suing in Alaska?
articles.summary: US government seeks to delay Alaska Senate result over concerns about two candidates with the same name.
articles.body:
The United States Department of Justice has filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of Alaska’s Senate election result if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses to Democrat Mary Peltola in the November 3 midterms.

The reason? Another candidate named Dan Sullivan is also on the ballot.

In a lawsuit filed on Thursday, the department argued that the second Sullivan, a retired teacher who registered as a Republican, is deliberately trying to confuse voters.

Alaska’s Supreme Court has already ruled that both candidates may remain on the ballot.

So who are the two Dan Sullivans, and what could the lawsuit mean for the election?

What is happening in Alaska’s US Senate race?

Senator Sullivan is seeking a third six-year term in the race against Peltola, a former congresswoman who became the first Alaska Native elected to the US House of Representatives in 2022.

Alaska has traditionally voted Republican in presidential elections. President Donald Trump won the state by roughly 13 percentage points in 2024, but this year’s Senate race appears more competitive.

In August’s primary, Peltola received 49.5 percent of the vote, compared with about 41 percent for Senator Sullivan.

Two other candidates advanced to the November 3 election: Daniel J Sullivan Jr and Gerald Heikes.

Dan S Sullivan was first elected to the US Senate in 2014 and was re-elected in 2020. He previously served as Alaska’s attorney general and commissioner of natural resources.

Daniel J Sullivan Jr is a retired elementary schoolteacher and a former US Forest Service employee from Petersburg in southeastern Alaska.

His entry into the race this year prompted accusations from Republicans that he was trying to confuse voters, something he has denied.

Alaska election officials initially disqualified him, but the state’s courts overturned the decision. In June, the Alaska Supreme Court allowed him to remain on the ballot.

The ballot identifies the incumbent as “Sullivan, Dan S (Registered Republican) Incumbent” and the other candidate as “Sullivan, Daniel J Jr” without a party designation, even though he has registered as a Republican.

Glenn Wright, a political science professor at the University of Alaska Southeast, told Al Jazeera that voters should have no problem recognising each candidate.

“The ballots are super, super, super clear about who the incumbent Dan Sullivan is,” he said.

But Forrest Nabors, chairman of the political science department at the University of Alaska Anchorage, said the similar names could still affect the result.

“It could swing the election if the election is close and the margin of voters who intend to re-elect the senator are confused and accidentally vote for the other candidate named Sullivan,” he told Al Jazeera.

Why has the Justice Department filed a lawsuit?

The Justice Department sued Alaska in federal court on Thursday, arguing that having two candidates with similar names could mislead voters.

It wants the state to be prevented from certifying the result if the Republican senator loses by fewer votes than his namesake receives, pending an investigation into possible voter confusion and whether voters mistakenly supported the wrong Sullivan.

The lawsuit cited the National Voter Registration Act, a federal law governing voter registration.

Nabors described the Justice Department’s intervention as “unusual” but said there could be circumstances in which federal action is justified.

“It’s perhaps not unreasonable,” he said, adding that federal intervention could be justified when an election is administered unfairly.

“Whether voters are confused and erroneously vote or not is a question that is hard to measure,” he added.

Wright questioned the basis of the lawsuit at all, however.

“The legal filing is either, you know, a filing in bad faith, or it’s a filing that misunderstands the way that Alaska’s election system operates,” he said.

How does Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system work?

Unlike most US states, Alaska allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference rather than voting for just one.

The four candidates with the most votes in the primary advance to the general election, regardless of party.

If nobody wins more than 50 percent of the first-choice votes, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated. Their votes are transferred to the next-ranked candidates still in the race. This continues until two candidates remain, and the one with the most votes wins.

Wright said the system helps prevent candidates with a smaller support base from splitting the vote.

“It’s supposed to eliminate the spoiler effect,” he explained.

For example, if a voter mistakenly chooses Daniel J Sullivan Jr but ranks the incumbent second, their vote could eventually transfer to the senator.

“The system is actually designed to cope with this sort of a thing,” Wright said.

However, voters are not required to rank every candidate, meaning some votes may not transfer.

Can the federal government block certification of the results?

The Justice Department may ask a federal court to intervene, but it may not independently stop Alaska from certifying the results.

The lawsuit seeks to delay certification if the Republican incumbent loses and votes cast for the other Dan Sullivan could have changed the outcome.

Derek Muller, an election law professor at the University of Notre Dame, questioned how officials would determine which candidate a voter intended to support.

“The best evidence that voters preferred one Sullivan over another is how they marked their ballots,” he wrote on the Election Law blog.

Muller also questioned the legal basis of the lawsuit.

The Justice Department cited the “findings and purposes” section of the National Voter Registration Act, which lists protecting “the integrity of the electoral process” among the law’s purposes.

But Muller argued that the department was treating that statement as a legal obligation, even though the law says nothing about which candidates may appear on a ballot.

He described the argument as “so absurdly thin” that there was “essentially no likelihood of success”.

He also questioned why the department had waited until days before the election to intervene when the dispute over the two candidates had been known for months.

Nabors said the case could still affect voters even if the courts do not decide it before election day.

“Whether the lawsuit is adjudicated in time, it will at least drive awareness of the problem among voters, which might limit the numbers of those who vote erroneously for the other Sullivan,” he told Al Jazeera.

No federal court has ordered Alaska to suspend certification.

What does this mean for the midterm elections?

Alaska’s Senate race could play a part in deciding which party controls the upper chamber of the US Congress.

Republicans now hold 53 of the Senate’s 100 seats while Democrats and two independents who caucus with them hold 47. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach 51 and secure a majority.

A 50-50 split would allow Vice President JD Vance to cast tie-breaking votes in the chamber.

“The defeat of Senator Sullivan would also take away an important senator from the Republican caucus. He has been influential in foreign policy and energy policy,” Nabors said.

Wright said the competitive race in such a traditionally Republican state reflects wider dissatisfaction with the Trump administration.

“The fact that the Alaska race has come to be competitive is a real indicator of how difficult the road is for a lot of Republican candidates in the current, kind of public opinion environment,” Wright said.

The lawsuit has also raised questions about whether the Trump administration could challenge certification in other states in which Republicans lose.

The Justice Department is already facing criticism over investigations and prosecutions involving Democratic opponents of Trump.

Federal agents have recently searched the home of Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar as part of an immigration fraud investigation. Omar has described the action as politically motivated.

Trump has acknowledged directing the Justice Department to file the Alaska lawsuit while his administration maintains that the action is intended to prevent voter confusion.

articles.title: After oil, internet? Iran plans to target Gulf's undersea cables
articles.summary: Iran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communication cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel launch fresh attacks, news agency
articles.body: Iran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communication cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel launch fresh attacks, news agency Reuters reported citing two senior Iranian security officials. This has raised the prospect of disruptions to internet services, financial transactions and cloud computing after disruptions at Strait of Hormuz sent oil supply shocks globally.The officials gave few details about how or where Iran might carry out such attacks. However, one said Tehran would seek to prevent repairs to damaged cables to prolong disruptions, including to internet connections."If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines ... from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones," Reuters quoted one of the officials saying.The official warned Washington not to "play with fire", adding that Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.Yadollah Javani, deputy head of political affairs for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.What could be the impactUndersea cables carry around 99% of global internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union. However, the global impact of any attacks in the Strait of Hormuz could be limited, as less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the waterway, said Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications research firm TeleGeography, the Reuters report said.The strait lies between Iran and Oman and connects the Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.Multiple cable cuts could slow internet services and disrupt financial transactions, e-commerce and cloud computing. The extent of the disruption would depend on how quickly operators could reroute traffic and whether alternative connections had enough capacity.Repairs could also prove difficult during a war, with higher insurance costs and delays in obtaining permission to enter territorial waters potentially slowing the process.The Red Sea could be a more significant target because it carries data between Europe, East Africa and Asia. Capacity routed through the region accounts for about 3% of global international demand and around 10% of traffic travelling between regions, Mauldin said.Iran could potentially have support from its Houthi allies in Yemen, although Tehran has made no public statement indicating plans to target cables in the Red Sea.Iran has already struck two Amazon Web Services facilities in the United Arab Emirates in March and damaged infrastructure near one of its facilities in Bahrain.You use AI every day. articles.title: New Zealand study suggests pine planting reduced annual streamflow by nearly 30% in one Waikato catchment and 4.7% in another
articles.summary: Converting grazed pasture to pine plantation can significantly reduce the amount of water flowing through streams, according to a hydrological modelling
articles.body: Converting grazed pasture to pine plantation can significantly reduce the amount of water flowing through streams, according to a hydrological modelling study of 2 afforested catchments in New Zealand’s Waikato region. Published in Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies in 2024, the study, titled Modelling the hydrological impact of afforestation in hill country catchments in New Zealand, used the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) to estimate the effects of land-use change. The researchers, Linh Hoang and Andrew Hughes, modelled a 29.7% reduction in mean annual streamflow in Mangaotama, where approximately 57% of the catchment was afforested. In Kiripaka, where about 9% was afforested, the modelled reduction was 4.7%. A third catchment, Whakakai, served as a native-forest control and had no land-use change. Increased evapotranspiration and reduced surface runoff were the main mechanisms behind the modelled decline. However, the size and timing of the changes varied, highlighting the need to consider model uncertainty when assessing the hydrological effects of plantation forestry.How researchers modelled pine afforestation in two Waikato catchmentsHoang and Hughes examined 3 hill-country catchments in the Waikato region, but only 2 underwent pasture-to-pine conversion. Mangaotama was approximately 57% afforested, while Kiripaka was about 9% afforested. Whakakai, which was covered by native forest, served as a control catchment without land-use change. Whakakai had no land-use change and served only as a native-forest control. The modelled streamflow reductions applied to the 2 afforested catchments, with a larger estimated effect in Mangaotama than in Kiripaka. The researchers used SWAT, a hydrological model that simulates how water moves through a catchment, to compare modelled streamflow under scenarios with and without land-use change. They evaluated the model against observed streamflow data from before and after the change. According to the paper, SWAT reproduced the magnitude, timing and variation of streamflow at daily and monthly scales, allowing the researchers to investigate how much of the observed change could be associated with afforestation.The best-fit model results indicated a 29.7% reduction in mean annual streamflow in Mangaotama. However, the estimated effect varied across the behavioural parameter sets, which represent different model configurations that met the researchers’ performance criteria. Across these sets, the median reduction was 20%, with a range of 12% to 32%. In Kiripaka, the modelled reduction was 4.7%. These differences show that the estimated hydrological effect varied with the extent of afforestation and the parameters used in the model.The researchers also identified limitations in the model’s representation of forest growth. SWAT produced a streamflow reduction immediately after planting, whereas observations showed a more gradual decline over approximately 7 years. The authors attributed this discrepancy to limitations in the model’s forest-growth representation. The model also overestimated post-change increases in streamflow in the other 2 catchments. In Whakakai, it predicted an increase of 24%, compared with an observed increase of 11%. In Kiripaka, it predicted an increase of 10.5%, while the observed change was approximately a 1% decline. These differences are important when interpreting the precision of the modelled estimates.Why pine plantations can reduce streamflowThe 2024 study identified increased evapotranspiration and reduced surface runoff as the main reasons for the modelled decline in streamflow. Evapotranspiration combines water evaporating from land and vegetation with water absorbed by plants and released into the atmosphere. Replacing short pasture with trees changes how rainfall is intercepted, stored and returned to the atmosphere, potentially leaving less water available to reach streams. The model also indicated a decline in groundwater flow in Mangaotama. Across the behavioural parameter sets, the median reduction was 30%, and more than 75% of the sets showed a decline. In Kiripaka, the median change was approximately −1%, indicating little overall change and considerable uncertainty about the direction of the effect. The findings therefore suggest a clearer modelled groundwater decline in the more heavily afforested catchment, rather than a uniform response across the study area.An earlier field study provides the observational evidence against which the later model was evaluated. Published in the New Zealand Journal of Marine and Freshwater Research in 2020, “The stream hydrology response of converting a headwater pasture catchment to Pinus radiata plantation” examined 23 years of data from Mangaotama, a steep pastoral catchment in the western Waikato. The researchers reported that approximately 62% of the catchment had been planted with pine. This differs slightly from the approximately 57% afforestation used in the 2024 modelling study. Seven years after planting, annual runoff was 380 mm lower than the researchers predicted it would have been if the catchment had remained in pasture. The 2024 model estimated a 29.7% reduction in mean annual flow for Mangaotama, broadly consistent with the approximately 32% reduction reported by the earlier field study. Because the 2020 observations were used to evaluate the later model, this agreement represents validation against field data, not independent confirmation from an unrelated catchment.The 2020 study also reported that peak flows fell by approximately 50%, while low flows appeared to decline by about 25%. The authors described the low-flow result as less clear. They linked the changes in peak flows and stormflow largely to canopy interception, which can reduce or delay the amount of rainfall reaching the ground. After 2 phases of plantation thinning, the difference between measured runoff and the pasture-based prediction narrowed to 129 mm, indicating that the hydrological response also changed with plantation management.What the Waikato findings mean for water and catchment managementThe studies show that converting pasture to pine plantation can alter the amount and timing of water flowing through streams. However, they do not establish that the same reduction will occur in every plantation or catchment. The modelled decline was substantially larger in Mangaotama, where afforestation was more extensive, than in Kiripaka, where only about 9% of the catchment was afforested. The implications for low flows also require caution. The 2020 field study suggested that low flows may have declined, but its authors described the result as less clear. The 2024 modelling paper likewise found that changes in baseflow were less consistent than changes in overall streamflow. The evidence therefore does not justify a general claim that pine afforestation will necessarily reduce low flows by a particular amount.The findings apply specifically to pasture-to-pine conversion in the catchments studied. They should not automatically be extended to other types of forestry, different land-use transitions or all catchments in New Zealand. The model’s limitations in representing forest growth and the uncertainty across parameter sets also affect how precisely the results can be applied elsewhere. For landowners and regional planners, assessing potential effects on water yield and interpreting model predictions alongside long-term streamflow measurements are reasonable considerations when evaluating proposed land-use changes. The study demonstrates the value of hydrological modelling, while also showing why model assumptions, field observations and local catchment conditions matter when estimating the effects of afforestation.You use AI every day. articles.title: A rare Nanotyrannus skeleton discovered by a Montana rancher in 2019 heads to auction for up to $9 million as scientists debate private fossil sales
articles.summary: A skeleton that looks like a small Tyrannosaurus rex is now standing in a Manhattan lobby, waiting for bidders.
articles.body: A skeleton that looks like a small Tyrannosaurus rex is now standing in a Manhattan lobby, waiting for bidders. It was unearthed in 2019 by a Montana rancher, and scientists have since confirmed it belongs to a different predator altogether, the Nanotyrannus. That confirmation ended a debate that had lasted for decades, and it has turned an unusual find into a headline lot. Its sale touches on a wider question, who should be able to dig up dinosaurs? Learn how it was found, how it differs from its famous cousin, and why scientists disagree about selling it.How Montana rancher Jodi Pierson discovered the Nanotyrannus skeleton on her land near a famous earlier findThe skeleton is nicknamed Jodi after Jodi Pierson, the rancher who found it on her land. Its discovery and excavation were the focus of the Discovery Channel documentary series "Dino Hunters" in 2020. The location is notable; the fossil lay some 8 miles (13 kilometres) from the site where the so-called Dueling Dinosaurs fossil was unearthed in 2006. That earlier find depicts a Nanotyrannus and a Triceratops together, which means one small stretch of Montana has produced two of the very few known skeletons of this predator.Why scientists doubted Nanotyrannus was a separate dinosaur until growth rings in its bones settled the debateThe argument dates back to 1942, when what is now considered the first Nanotyrannus head, known as the Cleveland Skull, was discovered. It is housed at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History. For decades, researchers wondered whether such fossils belonged to young Tyrannosaurus rex. In October 2025, new research concluded otherwise. Scientists examining growth rings inside preserved bones found fully formed adults, not juveniles, which established Nanotyrannus as a distinct genus. Cassandra Hatton, head of science and natural history at Sotheby's, told The Associated Press that, until the genus was proved, Tyrannosaurus rex was assumed to be the only apex predator of the Cretaceous period, some 67 million years ago. "We now know that they coexisted," she said, each occupying its own niche in the ecosystem.How Nanotyrannus differed from Tyrannosaurus rex in size, arm length, claws and teeth, and the prey it huntedMore than 150 key differences separate the two animals, and size is the most obvious. An adult Nanotyrannus reached about 18 feet (5.5 metres), roughly half the length of an adult Tyrannosaurus rex. Its forelimbs were longer than the famously stubby arms of its larger cousin, and its hand claws were bigger. The teeth also differed, Nanotyrannus had more of them, slender and almost bladelike, whereas those of Tyrannosaurus rex were thick and almost banana-shaped. Hatton likened the pair to a lion and a cheetah, telling the agency that the slender teeth slashed meat from faster prey, while the big, lumbering Tyrannosaurus rex went after slower animals and ate them whole. It is even possible, she said, that Tyrannosaurus rex ate Nanotyrannus.Jodi at Sotheby's, a skeleton almost 70 per cent complete, estimated at $6 million to $9 million, goes to auctionJodi was unveiled on Tuesday 13 October in the lobby of Sotheby's headquarters in Manhattan, ahead of an auction on 27 October with an estimate of $6 million to $9 million. The mounted skeleton stands 6.5 feet (2 metres) tall and stretches nearly 20 feet (6 metres) long. Hatton said it is almost 70 per cent complete, with a virtually complete skull and a jaw holding roughly 50 teeth. Sotheby's bills it as the "finest and most complete" Nanotyrannus skeleton currently available, a phrase that carries weight because only three skeletons are known. The Dueling Dinosaurs specimen, nicknamed Bloody Mary, is considered nearly 100 per cent complete but sits in the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences and is not for sale. The third is at the Burpee Museum of Natural History in Rockford, Illinois. The auction follows Sotheby's record $50.1 million sale of a Tyrannosaurus rex fossil this summer.Why the Society of Vertebrate Palaeontology opposes private sales of fossils like Jodi and how Sotheby's defends themThe Society of Vertebrate Palaeontology, an advocacy group of scientists, scholars and students, wants significant fossils like Jodi displayed in museums and other research institutions rather than sold privately. Hatton counters that the world might never have learned of Nanotyrannus without professional dinosaur hunters. "We absolutely need private diggers who invest their own money," she told the agency, pointing out that there are not enough universities and museums running field programmes. Stuart Sumida, the society's president and a biology professor at California State University San Bernardino, rejected that argument as a "blatant lie". He told The Associated Press that no peer-reviewed study can be published on specimens that are not held in the public trust, once such a fossil is in private hands, he said, it can never be studied, and generations will never see it again.You use AI every day. articles.title: Three released without charge after fatal Waterford arson attack
articles.summary: Three people - two women and one man - have been released, and one person remains in custody, gardaí say.
articles.body:
Three people, who were arrested in connection with a suspected arson attack which killed four family members in the Republic of Ireland, have been released, gardaí (Irish police) have said.

Philip and Kim English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford was set on fire earlier this month .

A man aged in his 20s and a woman in her 30s were previously charged in connection with the attack.

On Saturday, gardaí said three people - two women in their 30s and a man in his 50s - who were arrested on Tuesday have been released without charge.

A fourth person, a man in his 20s who was arrested on Thursday, remains in custody.

articles.title: Brazil’s Lula and Bolsonaro debate policy proposals before run-off
articles.summary: Polls indicate Brazil’s presidential candidates are neck and neck before Sunday’s voting.
articles.body:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro have focused on policy proposals in the final debate before their presidential run-off .

The candidates questioned each other on Friday, two days before the election, about Brazil’s economy, infrastructure and regional development.

Lula challenged his rival’s plan to take a “chainsaw” to public spending in a manner similar to that of Argentina’s libertarian president, Javier Milei.

“I’ll have the same job here [as Milei in Argentina] because you’re leaving the country bankrupt,” Bolsonaro responded.

Bolsonaro, son of former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro , accused the incumbent of allowing organised crime to expand, driving families into debt and not addressing the higher cost of living.

“He doesn’t know what hunger is,” Brazil’s first working-class president said of Bolsonaro, who responded, “Why are things so expensive?”

Lula questioned the senator’s experience, saying, “He doesn’t know Brazil.”

His challenger doubled down on presenting himself as a capable candidate who represented change for the country.

Friday’s debate in Rio de Janeiro, which was broadcast on TV Globo, was notably more diplomatic than their initial face-off on Sunday but also saw its share of personal attacks and tense moments.

Bolsonaro called Lula “Nine Fingers”, a pejorative nickname used by many of his supporters that references an accident the Brazilian president suffered during his time as a metalworker. The 80-year-old leader demanded an apology, which Bolsonaro gave him.

Lula in response called Bolsonaro a vigilante, referring to allegations that his rival has ties to paramilitary groups in Rio de Janeiro. Bolsonaro said he would classify those groups as “narcoterrorists”.

The third tense exchange was between Bolsonaro and the mother of a five-year-old who was killed in a shootout that involved a policeman who had the presidential candidate as his lawyer. Bolsonaro said he doesn’t believe his client was guilty.

Bolsonaro finished first in the initial round of voting on October 4 with 47 percent of the vote to Lula’s 45 percent.

A Datafolha institute survey published on Thursday suggested the pair are now tied with 50 percent support each, compared with Bolsonaro’s four-point lead in polls published two weeks ago.

Both candidates are expected to join supporters in the streets of Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo in their last campaign effort before Sunday’s run-off.

articles.title: Shropshire charity expects demand for Christmas present campaign
articles.summary: The campaign, run by Little Stars, is running from today until 4 December.
articles.body:
A Shropshire charity has said it expects demand to be high this year for its campaign which provides Christmas presents to struggling families.

Little Stars, which gives away free essentials to families in need, has launched Santa's Little Stars, which runs from Saturday 24 October to Friday 4 December.

The public is asked to donate new, unwrapped toys and gifts to donation points in Shrewsbury's Darwin shopping centre.

Donations are wrapped and given to children from birth to age 17, as well as pregnant women who are referred to the charity.

Little Stars said 2025 was its biggest campaign year to date, and it expected demand to continue to be high due to many families continuing to face financial pressures.

The charity launched Santa's Little Stars in 2020 and has given out more than 8,000 presents in that time, supporting more than 2,100 children.

It added that donations could be taken to collection points outside the Collective, The Entertainer, Home Bargains and Clarks Shoes.

articles.title: South Ribble Council charged after Paul FIddler killed by tree
articles.summary: South Ribble Council is being prosecuted over the death of Paul Fiddler, who died in Storm Darragh.
articles.body:
A council has been charged over the death of a football coach whose van was struck by a falling tree during Storm Darragh.

Paul Fiddler, who was in his 40s, died when the tree fell on his Citroen van as he drove along the A59 Longton Bypass in Hutton, Lancashire, on 7 December 2024.

The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) said South Ribble Borough Council was being prosecuted under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 in connection with his death.

No date had been set for the first court hearing, the HSE said.

The watchdog said the council had been charged under Section 3(1) of the act, following an investigation initially conducted with Lancashire Police.

Storm Darragh caused widespread disruption across the UK , with fallen trees, power cuts and events cancelled because of strong winds.

Following Fiddler's death, Lytham Town FC, where he was a coach, paid tribute to him on social media, describing him as a "legend" and a "true friend".

The club said: "A well loved coach, football player, gaffer but most of all a true friend."

South Ribble Borough Council has been approached for comment.

articles.title: A retired decorator had no idea his Pokémon cards were valuable until he read the local paper; now he earned Rs 19 crore after selling them at an auction house after keeping them in his attic for 15 years
articles.summary: Imagine finding out that the old cards in your attic are worth a fortune, all because of a small story in the local paper.
articles.body: Imagine finding out that the old cards in your attic are worth a fortune, all because of a small story in the local paper. That is what happened to a retired decorator from Woking, a town in England, who became a millionaire by selling his Pokémon card collection. He had no idea the cards were valuable until he read that a single card had sold for more than £6,000, and this one line in the newspaper made him look at his own collection in a new way.Let us know what happened with a father who earned millions with his cards kept in an old atticHow a Retired Decorator Made Rs 19 Crore From Pokémon Cards kept in his attic for 15 yearsA retired decorator from Woking in England has become a millionaire after selling his Pokémon card collection at auctionAccording to the BBC, the cards had been in his attic for 15 years, and he sold them at Ewbank's on Wednesday for £1.56 million or nearly Rs 19 to 20 crore. He had no idea the cards were worth anything until he read in his local newspaper about a single card that sold for more than £6,000.The man began collecting his cards when he was at schoolIn the late 1990s, his young son began collecting Pokémon cards and swapping them at school.The father thought they looked nice and wondered whether they might be a good investment.He explained, "When my son was young, in the late 1990s, he started getting cards and swapping them at school. I thought they looked nice and wondered whether they might be a good investment. He had his own cards, but he never got to touch these, I'm glad to say".He bought complete sets, some from a seller in Malaysia on eBay and the cards were kept sealed in bespoke binders and went up to the attic when his son lost interest. As he told the BBC, people always talk about finding treasure in the attic, and "in my case that is literally true."It came as a shock for the auction house as wellEwbank's, an auction house in Surrey, said staff were stunned when he brought in 42 sets. James Spooner, head of trading cards, said the cards were all in mint condition.The deck included legendary card collectionsThe top lot was a Legendary Collection Complete Master Set that included a near-mint Charizard card. articles.title: An Australian TV reporter was filming floods when he spotted a sinking four-wheel drive, swam out with a bystander and forced open a rear door to rescue the driver moments before the vehicle disappeared underwater
articles.summary: Not every hero wears a cape. Some simply hold a mic. Will Murray, an ABC reporter, was in Morayfield to cover the heavy rain and flooding.
articles.body: Not every hero wears a cape. Some simply hold a mic. Will Murray, an ABC reporter, was in Morayfield to cover the heavy rain and flooding. That’s when a four-wheel drive came through the flooded Buchanan Road, stalled and began to sink.Within seconds, the car was out of sight. Murray made a quick call to Triple Zero, handed the phone to a colleague and swam out. Daniel Hainey, a bystander, also jumped in to rescue the man. The incident happened in Morayfield, north of Brisbane, on Thursday, 22 October, where about 170 millimetres of rain had fallen since the morning. All three were safe after the rescue, which was captured on camera by Murray’s colleague.Unexpected heroesWill Murray was at the scene with camera operator Liz Pickering to cover the flooding. They were filming overlay footage of the flooded road when Murray saw the car enter the water.“I saw him drive in and immediately his car started floating downstream, so I rang Triple Zero,” the reporter recalled. The emergency operator asked him whether he could see the driver and whether the man could get free. Initially, Murray could see him, but then the driver disappeared from view. So Murray handed the phone to Pickering. “I made the call to jump in.”Daniel Hainey, who was out with his family nearby, had also noticed the vehicle. He did not realise anyone was inside until the window moved. By then, the car was sinking deeper. So he went into the water too.The rescueThe two men reached the car and tried the nearest door. It would not open. They moved to the back and looked for another way in. That’s when Murray tried the rear passenger door. He braced his feet against the car and pulled as hard as he could. Finally, the door swung open.He believes the rushing water helped by building pressure against the door. “I think water rushing in helped create some pressure to force the door open,” he told the broadcaster. The driver immediately got out, and the two men pulled him clear into shallower water. “All three of us gave each other a big hug and were just so relieved. It was very scary, but happy everyone is safe and relieved it is OK,” the reporter recalled.The man got lucky, but approach flooded roads with cautionEmergency services arrived about ten minutes after the rescue. The driver had not seen the warning signs. “I had no idea how deep it was, and that’s the lesson we keep hearing. It didn’t look particularly severe. But as you can see in the vision, the car completely disappears. It’s clearly very deep in the middle there,” Murray said.Hainey said the driver was “very, very lucky”. When asked about being called a hero, Murray quickly turned the attention towards emergency workers. He said the experience had given him a new respect for their work.The Queensland Fire Department has repeatedly warned residents about the dangers of floodwater and advises them to follow these safety guidelines:Never drive in floodwaters.Never swim or wade in floodwaters.Continue to monitor your local media for updated information and advice.For life-threatening emergencies, call Triple Zero (000).For storm- and flood-related property damage, call the State Emergency Service (SES) on 132 500.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang backed a Seattle lab with nearly 7 million GPU hours; its new AI model designs proteins up to 10 times faster and helps tackle pollution
articles.summary: The Jensen and Lori Huang Foundation, co-founded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his wife Lori recently provided the UW Medicine Institute for Protein
articles.body: The Jensen and Lori Huang Foundation, co-founded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his wife Lori recently provided the UW Medicine Institute for Protein Design (IPD) with a transformational computing grant totaling nearly 7 million GPU hours. The lab recently introduced RFD4-Proteina, an open, generative model co-developed by IPD and Nvidia. The model is claimed to design proteins up to 10 times faster and uses biomolecular reasoning to improve how well scientists can design new proteins with specific functions.Making RFD4-Proteina open will allow scientists around the world to build on its capabilities, explore more potential protein designs and move promising drug candidates into laboratory testing faster.“RFD4-Proteina will open the door to new solutions in medicine, sustainability, materials and biotechnology,” said David Baker, IPD director and professor of biochemistry at the University of Washington School of Medicine.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang gives AI computing power nearly 7 million GPU hours to Seattle LabEarlier this month, the Jensen and Lori Huang Foundation, granted totaling nearly 7 million hours of compute time, will accelerate the IPD’s development of open-source AI models for protein design. The models will enable the creation of molecules with applications in medicine, technology and sustainability.The in-kind grant provided access to graphics processing units. These specialized AI computing systems will cut algorithm learning and evaluation time from months to days. It will help IPD scientists solve complex protein-design problems in such areas as precision cancer therapeutics, durable vaccines, currently untreatable diseases and new enzymes that degrade environmental toxins like long-lasting hazardous chemicals and plastics. The compute power is provided through the Huang Foundation's partnership with CoreWeave using NVIDIA graphics processing units, or GPUs.“Most of the most important medicines of the future will come from proteins that have never existed," said Jensen Huang, co-president of the Huang Foundation. "For David Baker and the Institute for Protein Design, this path means training AI on tens of millions of molecular structures, learning from virtual experiments, and finding novel protein designs that have eluded nature. The Huang Foundation is providing researchers the compute to expand the frontiers of medicine, while ensuring that the resulting models, data, and tools are openly available to all."You use AI every day.
